source_read: In-press PDF (Article in press, Drug and Alcohol Dependence 2016; 14 pages), cited as PDF p. N. All pages read in a pdftotext -layout extraction; PDF pp. 3, 4 (Fig. 1), 7, 8 (Table 2, sideways, 200 dpi), 9 (Figs. 2-3, 200 dpi) and 10 (Fig. 4 and Table 3; Fig. 4 values and notes at 300 dpi) checked on rendered pages. Subgroup p values, meta-regression statistics and PEARRs recomputed; the treatment-at-baseline subgroups reproduced from the Fig. 4 study values (DerSimonian-Laird, logit scale). Funnel plots not published; no supplement.

claims.overstatement: One clause is not accurate as worded: 'the review did not appraise its cohorts'. The Methods say each selected study was critically appraised for inclusion with questions adapted from the Critical Appraisal Skills Programme (PDF p. 3, 2.2); what the review lacks is any reported appraisal result or risk-of-bias judgment, and appraisal was not used in the analysis. Suggested wording: 'the review reports no appraisal of its cohorts' (or: 'screened them for inclusion with a critical-appraisal checklist but reports no results'). Smaller points: (1) '21 cohorts ... followed for 3 to 50 years' fits 20 of them; the 21st (Lopez-Quintero et al., 2011, NESARC, 5,719 people) is a single general-population survey of lifetime cumulative probabilities, entered as 95.7% and set at 40 years for the annual-rate calculation, and it supplies the top of the 'about 20% to 96%' range. (2) 'remission was higher in cohorts followed longer' holds for the standard rate only (B 0.046, p 0.004); cohorts with lower retention also had higher standard rates (B -1.975, p 0.016), and neither relation was detectable for the conservative rate (follow-up p 0.235). (3) The '62% against 51%' comparison is the standard rate; on the conservative rate the direction reverses (27.9% without treatment at baseline against 38.2% with, p 0.388).
claims.note: All Fleury numbers in the statement and magnitude were found on the rendered pages: 21 cohorts, 12 alcohol, 4 heroin, 5 polysubstance (Fig. 1, PDF p. 4); published 2000-2015 (PDF p. 2); follow-up 3 to 50 years, mean 17 (PDF p. 4); 13 of 21 from the US by my count of Table 1 and PDF p. 4, so 'mostly from the US' holds; standard 54.4% (42.1-66.2), cohorts 19.6%-95.7%, I2 99.4%; conservative 35.0% (25.2-46.4), I2 99.5% (PDF p. 7; Fig. 4 prints 0.351, 0.252-0.464); treatment at baseline 15 cohorts 0.511 against 6 cohorts 0.624, p 0.421 (Table 2, PDF p. 8); B 0.046, p 0.004 (Table 3, PDF p. 10). 'Recruited through treatment' paraphrases Table 2's 'all or the majority ... in treatment at baseline' (the Discussion calls them 15 clinical samples). Reproducing Table 2 from the Fig. 4 values with a common tau2 (1.34) gives 0.511 (0.366-0.654) and 0.624 (0.394-0.810), p 0.41, when the six cohorts without treatment at baseline are Moss 2010, Lopez-Quintero 2011, Trim 2013, Penick 2010, Vaillant 2003 and Galai 2003. So the 62% includes the lifetime NESARC projection, and without it the six-cohort figure would fall to about 49% (my calculation, separate tau2; approximate). Penick's community sample was drawn partly from municipal alcohol treatment clinics (Table 1). 'Treatment during follow-up was not analysed' is supported (PDF p. 11). 'Describes no particular time point' is a fair reading of a pool of final-follow-up proportions from 3 years to a lifetime projection; the authors themselves present it as remission reached after a mean of 17 years of follow-up. Balance: the authors read the same figures as only a third to half remitting, with annualized rates of 6.8%-9.1%, and as support for treating SUDs as long-term disorders (PDF pp. 1, 11-12). The claim's 'a large share' is not wrong for 35%-54%, but the review's own reading is the opposite emphasis. Nothing in Fleury supports 'many of them without treatment': treatment was not analysed, and 15 of 21 cohorts started in treatment.

anchors.locator: Methods > 2.1 Search strategy and study inclusion criteria
anchors.extracted: Medline, PubMed, EMBASE, PsycINFO, a hand search of 19 addiction journals and reference lists; studies published January 2000 to December 2015, from OECD countries, in English or French; observational studies of adults with an SUD at baseline, followed at least three years with two or more data collections, or with lifetime cumulative remission estimates; remission over at least six months. Excluded: samples not all with an SUD, groups such as homeless people, indigenous peoples or veterans, trials and studies of experimental or substitution treatment.

anchors.locator: Methods > 2.2 Screening and data extraction, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Two reviewers screened independently (96% agreement on 10% of records); each selected study was critically appraised for inclusion with questions adapted from the Critical Appraisal Skills Programme; two members extracted data with a standardized form. No appraisal results are reported anywhere in the paper.

Only final-follow-up data were used. Standard rate: people in continuous remission (over six months) at final follow-up divided by the baseline sample minus those who died, were lost or no longer met inclusion criteria. Conservative rate: the same numerator divided by the whole baseline sample.

8,855 records screened, 119 full texts, 21 studies (12 alcohol, 4 heroin, 5 polysubstance). One study gave lifetime cumulative probabilities for 5,719 people; 20 followed people at two or more waves. Final follow-up 3 to 50 years (mean 17, median 13); retention 47%-98% excluding deaths (mean 80%), 21%-96% including them (mean 67%). 8 of 12 alcohol studies from the US; heroin studies from the US, England, Australia and Slovakia; polysubstance 4 US, 1 Sweden.

anchors.locator: Results > 3.3 Remission rates from SUDs, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Standard remission rates ranged 19.6%-95.7%; random-effects pooled 54.4% (95% CI 42.1-66.2) after a weighted mean 17.9 years (SD 14.0) of follow-up; I2 99.4%, tau2 1.3, Q 3337.3 on 20 df; leave-one-out 50.1%-56.4%; annualized pooled rate 9.1% (8.4-9.8).

Conservative rates ranged 15.5%-95.7%; pooled 35.0% (25.2-46.4) after a weighted mean 16.9 years (SD 13.4); I2 99.5%; leave-one-out 30.9%-36.3%; without the lifetime NESARC study 30.9% (26.1-36.1); annualized 6.8% (6.3-7.4). The authors judge true remission to lie between the two rates (standard inflates, conservative underestimates).

Study standard rates from 0.196 (Galai 2003) to 0.957 (Lopez-Quintero 2011, a lifetime estimate combining 0.91 alcohol, 0.97 cannabis, 0.998 cocaine); pooled 0.544 (0.421-0.662). Conservative pooled printed 0.351 (0.252-0.464); Lopez-Quintero again 0.957, with a note giving 37%, 66% and 76%.

anchors.locator: Table 2, Treatment at baseline rows and notes
anchors.extracted: Standard rate: all or most in treatment at baseline (15 studies) 0.511 (0.364-0.656) against not (6) 0.624 (0.390-0.812), Q 0.648, df 1, p 0.421. Conservative rate: 0.382 (0.259-0.522) against 0.279 (0.136-0.487), Q 0.747, p 0.388 (printed df 2; p corresponds to 1 df). Note: two of the six are population samples in which some people were in treatment. No categorical factor was significant.

Standard rate on follow-up duration B 0.046 (SE 0.016; 0.014 to 0.08), R2 analog 0.30, Q 8.09, p 0.004; on retention B -1.975 (SE 0.821), p 0.016; sex and age not related. Conservative rate: follow-up B 0.020, p 0.235; retention p 0.060.

Characteristics that could have explained heterogeneity but were not tested, because the studies had not recorded them as variables, include criminal activity, unemployment, social support, co-occurring mental disorders and treatment received over time; 15 clinical, 4 community and 2 population samples; eight studies used self-reported SUD.

Few studies; OECD and English or French only, mostly US samples except heroin; remission defined from abstinence to controlled use and over 6 months to 10 years; rates based on status at final follow-up only, not on trajectories.

anchors.locator: Abstract, Results and Conclusions; 4.2 Conclusion (PDF pp. 11-12)
anchors.extracted: The authors read the results as 35.0%-54.4% achieving remission after a mean 17 years of follow-up, few remissions in any year (6.8%-9.1%), and support for viewing SUDs as more often chronic or long-term than acute for a substantial number of people.

key_findings.correction: Values match Table 2. Worth adding to the note: reproducing the subgroups from Fig. 4 (common tau2 1.34) identifies the six cohorts without treatment at baseline as Moss 2010, Lopez-Quintero 2011, Trim 2013, Penick 2010, Vaillant 2003 and Galai 2003; the 0.624 includes the lifetime NESARC projection (0.957), and without it this group is about 0.49 (editors' calculation); Penick's sample came partly from municipal treatment clinics.

reporting_issues.note: PDF p. 10, Discussion 6th paragraph, against Table 2 (0.464 any SUD, 0.695 dependence only).
Recomputed: Q 0.747 gives p 0.387 on 1 df and 0.688 on 2 df.
Recomputed: PEARR 9.11% weighting by final N and 6.85% by baseline N; 1 - exp(-0.091 x 17.9) = 0.80, 1 - exp(-0.068 x 17.9) = 0.70; implied constant rates 4.4% and 2.5%.

risk_of_bias.note: AMSTAR 2 critically low: critical items 2, 4, 7, 9 and 11 not met. Item 9's note correctly says studies were appraised only as a gate for inclusion with no results reported, which is also why the claim's 'did not appraise' needs rewording. The card's baseline sum (21,370) recomputed.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial. Recomputed ln2/0.091 = 7.6 and ln2/0.068 = 10.2 years.

missed: The treatment-at-baseline contrast (key finding 4) rests on the lifetime NESARC projection: by reconstruction from Fig. 4 the six cohorts without treatment at baseline are Moss 2010, Lopez-Quintero 2011, Trim 2013, Penick 2010, Vaillant 2003 and Galai 2003, and without Lopez-Quintero their standard rate is about 49%, below the treatment cohorts' 51% (editors' calculation; the review does not list the groups).
